title: Capt. Nathaniel Hart
summary: Transylvania Company proprietor Nathaniel Hart settled White Oak Springs near Boonesborough in Madison County in 1779 and was killed nearby in 1782.
bodyMarkdown:
Nathaniel Hart was one of the investors who tried to buy much of Kentucky from the Cherokee. According to the [Kentucky Historical Society marker for his home](https://history.ky.gov/markers/home-of-capt-nathaniel-hart), he was born in 1734 in Hanover County, Virginia. He became a proprietor of the Transylvania Company and a key figure in its land purchase from the Cherokee.

## The Transylvania Purchase

The [Transylvania Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) was led by the North Carolina lawyer [Richard Henderson](/stories/richard-henderson/). It had [nine principal partners](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony), including Nathaniel Hart and his brother Thomas, and Nathaniel was active in Cherokee diplomacy.

On March 17, 1775, at Sycamore Shoals on the Watauga River, the company signed deeds with Cherokee leaders for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky and Cumberland rivers. About [1,200 Cherokee attended](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) the talks, led by figures such as Attakullakulla, Oconostota and Dragging Canoe. The company paid in trade goods and silver valued at about £10,000.

Not all Cherokee agreed. Dragging Canoe protested the sale and warned of bloodshed over the land. He later led Cherokee resistance to the settlers. The purchase also had no royal or colonial approval.

Virginia rejected it and in December 1776 made the region Kentucky County. North Carolina later granted the partners 200,000 acres in Powell's Valley in 1783 as compensation.

## White Oak Springs

The KHS marker says Hart came to Boonesborough in 1775, the company's main settlement. In 1779 he settled White Oak Springs, also called Hart's Station. Some Dutch families from Pennsylvania joined him there. The marker says the old log house he built is the oldest house still standing in Madison County.

The years around Boonesborough were violent. Cherokee territory [reached](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) into Kentucky's hunting grounds, and Shawnee and allied Cherokee forces, often supported by British agents during the Revolution, attacked Transylvania settlements. The largest attack was the 13-day siege of Boonesborough in September 1778, led by the Shawnee leader Blackfish. For Boonesborough's leaders, see [Col. Richard Callaway of Boonesborough](/stories/col-richard-callaway-of-boonesborough/).

## Death and family

In 1782 Hart was killed near his house; the marker says he was killed "by Indians." He was buried across the road. The marker does not name the attackers' nation.

His family stayed prominent. His daughter Susannah married Isaac Shelby, who became Kentucky's first and fifth governor. See [Isaac Shelby, "Old Kings Mountain"](/stories/isaac-shelby-old-kings-mountain/) for that story.

## Kentucky today

The KHS marker stands about a mile south of the main entrance to Fort Boonesborough State Park in Madison County. The old log house the marker describes stands nearby. For the county's later seat, see [Richmond](/stories/richmond-from-millers-barn/).
